column4: The section’s completion-and-guidance pairing is stated in one clause: God completes His favor and guides the Prophet to a straight path.
God’s completed favor is joined to finding guidance after the direction of prayer is turned, exactly the section’s path-favor relation.
The perfection of religion and completion of God’s favor make the section’s sense of a benefit brought fully to its end explicit.
Joseph and the House of Jacob receive a favor completed across a family, sharpening the collective “those upon whom You bestowed favor.”
After the ablution instructions, God says He intends to complete His favor; ritual cleansing is a concrete mode of completed benefaction.
Shade, shelters, garments, and protection are given so that God may complete His favor; the verse shows completion through sustained care.
Abraham is grateful for God’s favors, then is chosen and guided to a straight path, joining the section’s thankful recipient to its path-favor.
Those who hold fast receive mercy and bounty and are guided to God on a straight path, making mercy the source of guided favor.
This ayah promises guidance to a straight path; 4:69 immediately identifies its companions as people God favored.
Those obeying God are with people upon whom God bestowed favor, completing 4:68’s straight-path promise in Fatiha’s own terms.
Completing the numbered days, magnifying God for His guidance, and giving thanks form a compact counterpart to completed favor, path, and praise.
The former enemies recall God’s favor in joining their hearts and saving them from the Fire; a communal gift is made a means of guidance.
God conferred favor on believers by sending a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches; the favor is explicitly a guided, repaired community.
The prophets are those God favored, and hearing the Merciful’s signs makes them fall prostrate and weep: received favor answers in worship.
God has lavished His favors, outward and hidden, upon people; the fullness of asbagha makes the section’s completed and increased gift concrete.
“Tell of your Lord’s favor” directly realizes the section’s account of hamd as speaking the giver’s benefits before others.
Those brought to the Garden praise God for having guided them there; hamd returns at the end of the path.
The believers’ Lord guides them by faith; 10:10 gives the praise with which their Garden speech ends.
The last word of the people of the Garden is praise to God, Lord of the worlds, explicitly returning to Fatiha’s opening hamd.
Abraham says hamd for the sons God granted him in old age, a direct instance of praise that names the giver’s particular gifts.
David and Solomon receive knowledge and answer together with hamd for God’s preference of them, displaying the recipient’s public acknowledgement.
After rescue on the Ark, Noah is told to say hamd to God who saved them; deliverance is answered by praise rather than self-credit.
The people of the Garden praise God for removing grief, a final acknowledgment of a received and completed rescue.
The inheritors of the Garden say hamd because God fulfilled His promise and gave them the land, matching praise after a realized gift.
On mounting ship or animal, people are to remember their Lord’s favor and glorify Him; a received means of travel becomes voiced acknowledgment.
Abraham’s public account names the Lord who created him and then guides him, embodying praise as recounting the giver’s acts.
In the same account, Abraham names the Lord who feeds and gives drink, a concrete benefit presented before others.
Joseph publicly says that his Lord dealt kindly with him by bringing him from prison and his family from the desert, recounting received good.
Joseph follows that recital by addressing his Lord as giver of authority and knowledge, returning the favor’s source to God.
Solomon asks to be enabled to give thanks for the favor bestowed on him and his parents and to do a righteous deed in response.
The sudden gift is called a favor from Solomon’s Lord and a test of gratitude or ingratitude, making the recipient’s answer the issue.
Moses answers God’s favor upon him with a moral pledge not to support criminals; gratitude takes the form of changed action.
The maturing child asks to be enabled to thank God for the favor upon himself and his parents and to act rightly.
After the gifts to David and Solomon in the preceding ayat, their household is commanded to work in gratitude, though few servants are grateful.
The sacrificial animals feed both giver and needy person and are made subject to people so that they may give thanks: benefit passes on and returns as gratitude.
God’s subjection of the animals is said to let people magnify Him for guidance, joining a received provision to praise and the way.
The people of the House are told to worship its Lord; 106:4 names the food and safety that ground this answer.
The Lord feeds them against hunger and secures them from fear, specifying the benefits to which 106:3 makes worship the response.
The Prophet is told that God has given him abundant good, a concise scene of divine gift before the answering worship in 108:2.
Prayer and sacrifice to the Lord follow the announced gift in 108:1, giving the section’s benefit-and-response sequence a compact form.
Lot’s rescue is called a favor from God, followed by the statement that He thus rewards whoever is grateful.
The saved speaker says that without the favor of his Lord he would have been among the brought forth, explicitly recognizing rescue as niʿmah.
A company in the Garden says God conferred favor on them and protected them from the scorching punishment, turning salvation into collective acknowledgment.
God promises that gratitude will bring increase; this is the section’s named secondary sense of enʿama as giving more, tied to 14:6’s recalled favor.
The parable contrasts one unable to act with one given good provision who spends it openly and secretly, then says hamd belongs to God; received good is passed on and praised.
People cannot count God’s favors; this places a limit beside the section’s picture of hamd as recounting the giver’s benefits.
After an inventory of provision, the ayah says people cannot count God’s favor and calls humankind unjust and ungrateful.
The command to remember God’s favor asks who besides Him provides from heaven and earth, identifying the giver behind every provision.
Every favor people have is from God; when harm comes, they call on Him, making the source of benevolence explicit.
Believers are told to eat the good things God provided and thank Him if they worship Him, directly joining provision, thanks, and service.
Eating God’s lawful good provision is followed by the command to thank His favor if He alone is worshipped.
The formerly few and fearful are reminded that God sheltered, strengthened, and provided good things for them so that they might give thanks.
God’s victory at Badr while the believers were weak is followed by the call to be mindful of Him so that they may be grateful.
God establishes people on earth and gives them means of livelihood, while exposing how little thanks they give.
Moses is told to take what he has been given and be among the grateful, making receipt and response explicit.
In land and sea darkness, people promise to be grateful if God saves them; the threatened rescue makes gratitude a vowed response to favor.
Passengers facing storm call on God sincerely and promise gratitude if He saves them, staging a recipient’s proper answer in extremity.
Abraham asks for fruit provision for his family near the Sacred House so that they may give thanks; sustenance and gratitude are deliberately paired.
The sea is made subservient for food, adornment, travel, and seeking bounty, expressly so that people may be grateful.
God brings people out knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts so that they may give thanks.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are gifts from God, and the verse rebukes the small amount of thanks they receive.
After forming the human and giving spirit, hearing, sight, and hearts, God notes how little gratitude people offer.
The fruit of revived land and what human hands make are given for eating, and the ayah asks why they do not give thanks.
Night for rest and day for sight are God’s bounty to people, yet most do not give thanks.
God subjects the sea for ships and the seeking of His bounty so that people may be grateful.
The sweetness of drinking water is presented as a gift God could have made bitter, followed by the question why people do not give thanks.
God gives hearing, sight, and hearts and says people give little thanks, another precise gift-to-response relation.
Out of mercy God made night and day for rest and seeking bounty, expressly so that people may be grateful.
Winds bring mercy, moving ships and enabling the search for bounty, so that people may give thanks.
The alternation of night and day is made for the person who wants to remember or be grateful, making time itself a received aid to response.
God tells Moses that He had already conferred favor on him another time; the following narrative details that sustaining care.
God tells believers to remember His favor when hostile people tried to stretch out their hands against them and He held those hands back; protection reverses the hand-image.
Joseph calls his monotheism part of God’s favor upon him and people, then notes that most people are not grateful.
God’s bounty and mercy are made the ground for rejoicing, a positive reception of the giver’s favor rather than its denial.
Believers receive a double share of mercy and a light by which to walk, joining mercy-as-benefaction to a path.
God honors the children of Adam, carries them on land and sea, provides good things, and grants preference; the catalog invites the hamd-like naming of benefits.
The people of Sheba are given gardens, provision, a good land, and a forgiving Lord, then summoned to eat from their Lord’s provision and give thanks.
At the completion of victory in 110:1–2, the Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord with praise and seek forgiveness, answering an accomplished gift with hamd.
The refrain asks which of the Lord’s favors the two addressees will deny; it is the rhetorical reverse of recounting favors in hamd.
After the creation signs, the refrain asks which favors of the Lord will be denied, pressing acknowledgment of the giver.
The refrain returns after the Lordship of the two easts and wests, making denial of the displayed favor the named opposite response.
After the two seas and their barrier, the refrain asks which favors of the Lord will be denied.
Pearls and coral are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors, turning a concrete gift into acknowledgment.
The mountain-like ships are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors, naming the recipient’s contrary response.
After all perish and the Lord remains, the refrain asks which of His favors will be denied.
The refrain follows the claim that every creature asks Him and that He is each day upon an affair, keeping dependence on the giver in view.
The warning that God will attend to humans and jinn is followed by the refrain against denying His favors.
After the challenge to escape the bounds of heaven and earth, the refrain again makes denial of the Lord’s favors the opposite of acknowledgment.
The punishment scene is followed by the refrain, so even the boundary of power is framed as a favor that must not be denied.
After the sky is split, the refrain asks which of the Lord’s favors will be denied.
The refrain returns after the Day when no human or jinn is asked of sin, retaining the surah’s insistence on recognizing the Lord’s favors.
After criminals are known by their marks, the refrain asks which favors of the Lord will be denied.
The Hell scene is followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors, making judgment a boundary for how favor is received.
The promise of two gardens to one who fears standing before the Lord is followed by the refrain against denying His favors.
The two branching gardens are followed by the refrain, so their abundance is explicitly held before the addressees for acknowledgment.
The two flowing springs are followed by the refrain against denial of the Lord’s favors.
The paired fruits of the gardens are followed by the refrain, turning enumerated abundance into a demand for acknowledgment.
The near fruits and brocade couches are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
The garden companions are followed by the refrain, continuing the surah’s repeated reversal of hamd into denial.
The two dark-green gardens are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
The two gushing springs are followed by the refrain, making their provision a named favor to acknowledge.
Fruits, dates, and pomegranates are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
The two dark-green gardens are followed by the refrain, continuing the inventory of received gifts.
The two gushing springs are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
Fruits, dates, and pomegranates are followed by the refrain, turning enumerated abundance into a demand for acknowledgment.
The fair and beautiful garden companions are followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
The companions sheltered in pavilions are followed by the refrain, keeping the contrast between favor and denial explicit.
Their untouched state is followed by the refrain against denying the Lord’s favors.
The final green cushions and fine carpets are followed by the refrain, closing the gift inventory before the surah’s blessing.
The giver of charity must not follow it with mann or injury; this directly forbids turning an extended good into a burden on its recipient.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, giving the boundary that 2:262–264 draw around benefaction.
Believers are forbidden to void charity by mann and injury or display; it is the Qur’anic scene closest to the section’s favor held over another.
Those who feed the needy say they seek neither recompense nor thanks, the inverse of using a gift to demand recognition from its recipient.
Giving beloved food to needy person, orphan, and captive makes the section’s hand-to-hand delivery of good concrete; 76:9 states its motive.
Pharaoh cites having raised Moses as a child as leverage; 26:22 names this claimed favor as reproach.
Moses calls Pharaoh’s claimed upbringing a favor he keeps holding over him, the exact dramatic scene of a benefit turned into mann.
People hold their Islam over the Prophet as a favor, but the ayah reverses it: God favored them by guiding them to faith.
“Do not grant a favor seeking more” sets a boundary around benefaction, linking the section’s dictionary senses of mann and of giving an increase.
The truly giving person has no favor owed to him for repayment, opposing a giver who keeps an account over a recipient.
The giver seeks only the face of the highest Lord, completing 92:19’s contrast with transactional or boastful benefaction.
Those who love to be praised for what they did not do form the false counterpart to hamd rightly directed to the real giver.
When enriched, the human says that his Lord has honored him; the verse tests the easy identification of a good condition with self-validating status.
The next ayah reverses the condition when provision is restricted and the human says he has been humiliated, exposing a distorted reading of favor.
Those given more provision refuse to return it to those under their authority so they become equal, and the ayah calls this denial of God’s favor.
When God gives them bounty after their pledge in 9:75, they become miserly and turn away; the received gift does not pass on as promised.
They resent only that God and His messenger enriched them from bounty, a hostile answer to received provision.
Those who exchange God’s favor for disbelief enact the direct opposite of the section’s thankful acknowledgment.
God does not change a favor He has bestowed until people change themselves, marking the moral boundary by which a favor can be lost.
When God removes harm after 16:53’s assertion that every favor is from Him, some people associate others with Him instead of answering the giver.
People recognize God’s favor and then deny it; the ayah names the reversal of both knowledge and grateful response.
A city secure and abundantly provisioned disbelieves God’s favors, then tastes hunger and fear; a good condition is undone by denial.
When God bestows favor on a human, he turns away and becomes remote; this is the opposite posture to hamd.
A person calls God in hardship, then forgets that appeal once God grants a favor; relief is received without lasting acknowledgment.
After receiving a favor, the person says it came through his own knowledge, substituting self-credit for naming the giver.
If mercy is tasted and then withdrawn, the human is despairing and ungrateful, showing a response governed by possession rather than the giver.
After adversity, tasting naʿmāʾ makes the human boast that evils have gone; the pleasant state becomes self-exultation.
After the rescue for which people pledged gratitude in 6:63, they associate partners with God instead.
Once God saves the passengers who vowed gratitude in 10:22, they transgress on earth, reversing their promised response.
When danger at sea is removed, people turn away despite having called on God; rescue becomes forgotten favor.
When people taste mercy they turn to their Lord, yet some associate partners after relief, splitting the source of the gift.
God distributes rain among people so they may remember, but most refuse anything but ingratitude; a shared benefit meets kufr.
Sheba turns away from the thankful land of 34:15, so its gardens are exchanged for bitter and scant growth.
The replacement of Sheba’s bounty is said to recompense their ingratitude, completing the reversal of 34:15.
The garden-owner is told he should have said “what God wills” on entering his garden; wealth that speaks for itself is corrected by attribution to its giver.
The command exposes people who disbelieve in what God has given them while enjoying it, a direct failure of received provision.
When people taste mercy they rejoice, but when evil reaches them for what their hands earned they despair; their response tracks the gift rather than its source.
After giving spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision, God asks whether people will believe falsehood and deny His favor.
They promise that, if God gives bounty, they will give charity and be righteous; 9:76 shows their breach after receiving it.
Israel is told to remember the favor God bestowed and fulfill His covenant, connecting received favor to a responsive obligation.
After pardoning Israel for the calf, God says perhaps they will give thanks; forgiveness becomes a particular favor requiring response.
God revives Israel after their death so that they may give thanks, framing restoration itself as benefaction.
The favor of God and the Book and wisdom sent down are to be remembered; guidance is a gift that instructs its recipient.
Believers are told to remember God’s favor and the covenant binding them, like 2:40 joining a gift to a faithful answer.
Moses asks his people to remember God’s favor in making prophets and kings among them and giving them what others had not received.
God tells Jesus to remember His favor upon him and his mother, then recounts its works; the giver Himself enumerates benefactions.
God is full of bounty toward people, yet most do not give thanks, stating the blessing-and-response issue without a single material scene.
Moses tells his people to remember God’s favor in rescuing them from Pharaoh; 14:7 names gratitude and increase as the answer.
Noah is called a grateful servant, providing a concise model of the recipient’s stance even though the specific gifts are left in the wider Noah narrative.
Israel’s rescue from the enemy and the provision of manna and quails form a communal scene of received sustenance under their Lord’s care.
Abraham adds that the Lord heals him when ill, extending his public account of received care beyond food and guidance.
Abraham hopes that the Lord will forgive his fault on Judgment Day, treating forgiveness as part of the beneficent Lord he publicly names.
God is possessive of bounty toward people, yet most do not give thanks; the verse universalizes the response issue.
The gifts of wind, molten copper, and jinn service to Solomon supply the concrete benefactions to which 34:13 answers with grateful work.
The sea provides fresh water, food, adornment, travel, and pursuit of bounty; its inventory invites the response of gratitude developed elsewhere in the section.
The dead earth revived and made to yield grain begins the provision scene that ends in 36:35’s question about gratitude.
Gardens, date palms, grapevines, and springs continue the concrete gift inventory completed by 36:35.
The question “which favors of your Lord will you dispute?” uses a favor-word to confront the opposite of acknowledging the benefactor.
Jonah is rescued from an exposed state when favor from his Lord reaches him, a narrative recognition of saving benefaction.
Questioning people about al-naʿīm turns the section’s “good state” sense of the root into accountable, rather than self-owned, ease.
Believers rejoice in favor and bounty from God and in the assurance that He does not waste the believers’ reward.
God asks what He would gain by punishing people if they give thanks and believe, placing gratitude among the decisive responses to His dealing.
God commands iḥsān and giving to kin, a practical counterpart to the section’s dictionary account of inʿām as conveying good to another.
Feeding in a day of severe hunger gives the section’s extended-hand image a concrete human scene.
The orphan near of kin is one recipient of the food in the preceding ayah, specifying the relational destination of benefaction.
The needy person in dust is the other recipient in the food-giving scene, keeping the act directed toward one in need.
The one who does not urge feeding the poor stands at the boundary of the section’s image of good actually delivered to another.
When told to spend from what God provided them, deniers refuse to feed one whom God could feed, withholding received provision from need.
God singles out whom He wills for His mercy and is possessor of great bounty, naming mercy and bounty as gifts from one source.
The Qur’an comes as admonition, healing, guidance, and mercy for believers, a nonmaterial form of the favorable path in the section.
The Messenger is sent as mercy to the worlds, making mercy itself a communal divine benefaction.
